narrative:
The model determined that you have roughly a 70% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this predicted risk led to the rejection of your application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of accepted students (around the 6th decile). These consistently low academic standings signaled to the model a higher likelihood of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 37 was the next most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. This score is almost exactly at the average of students who were accepted, so it slightly improved the model’s outlook and pulled the prediction back toward passing.

Taken together, the two weak decile rankings outweighed the solid LSAT result, producing the 70% failure probability that caused the denial.

You should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise it meaningfully. Many students improve their bar passage odds by addressing these exact gaps before reapplying. (198 words)
